lesson.title: Hier j'ai… Story Drills
lesson.subtitle: Narrate a past day in passé composé sentences with avoir.

hook.title: Narrating a Full Day in the Passé Composé
hook.content: Every converted verb from Topic 3's -ation engine (visiter, confirmer, organiser, réserver, célébrer, préparer) forms its past participle in -é (visité, confirmé, organisé, réservé, célébré, préparé) — and sounds 100% identical to its infinitive!

footnotes.title: How context distinguishes j'ai visité (/vizite/) from je vais visiter (/vizite/)
footnotes.content: Because visité and visiter are both pronounced /vizite/, the auxiliary in front of it does 100% of the time-travel work: je vais visiter (future) vs. j'ai visité (past)!

pattern.title: The Auxiliary Is the Time Machine: je vais /vizite/ vs. j'ai /vizite/
pattern.content: In writing, after je veux / je vais write -er (visiter); after avoir (j'ai / tu as) write -é (visité)!
pattern.linguist_note: Homophony of -er (/e/), -é (/e/), and -ez (/e/) makes pre-verbal auxiliaries the primary carriers of tense.
pattern.trap_note: Remember: after a conjugated verb (je veux / je vais), write -er; after avoir (j'ai / nous avons), write -é!

exercises.prompt: Contrast the written endings of /vizite/ and /paʁle/ by what precedes them:

matching_pairs.english: After j'ai / tu as / nous avons (participle)
After vous in the present (2nd pl.)

exercises.target_answer: visiter / parler (-er), visité / parlé (-é), visitez / parlez (-ez)
exercises.meaning: After je veux / je vais (infinitive), After j'ai / tu as / nous avons (participle), After vous in the present (2nd pl.)

exercises.prompt: Choose the correct written pair for 'I am going to reserve' vs. 'I reserved':
exercises.meaning: After vais → -er infinitive; after ai → -é participle
exercises.explanation: Both sound like /ʁezɛʁve/, but vais takes -er and ai takes -é!

exercises.prompt: Write the past sentence: 'Yesterday, I visited Paris' (Hier, j'ai + visit + Paris):
exercises.explanation: After j'ai, visiter wears its -é participle ending: visité.

exercises.idea: yesterday I spoke with my friend and we ate at the restaurant
cues: Yesterday I spoke with my friend → Hier, j'ai parlé avec mon ami
and we ate at the restaurant → et nous avons mangé au restaurant
idea_parts: first event → Hier, j'ai parlé avec mon ami
second event → et nous avons mangé au restaurant
exercises.target_answer: Hier, j'ai parlé avec mon ami et nous avons mangé au restaurant
exercises.meaning: Yesterday, I spoke with my friend and we ate at the restaurant
exercises.explanation: Both parlé and mangé take -é after avoir.

diagnosis.cue: After j'ai and nous avons, write parlé and mangé with -é.

exercises.prompt: Listen and write the whole sentence.
exercises.spoken: J'ai préparé le dîner et j'ai invité mes amis
exercises.target_answer: J'ai préparé le dîner et j'ai invité mes amis
exercises.meaning: I prepared dinner and invited my friends
exercises.explanation: Two -ation engine verbs in the past: préparé and invité.
exercises.affirmation: You wrote -é on both préparé and invité after j'ai!

summary.outcome: Narrate sequences of past events with avoir and distinguish homophonous -er, -é, and -ez in writing.

use_example.german: Hier, j'ai réservé une table et nous avons célébré.
use_example.english: Yesterday, I reserved a table and we celebrated.

summary.takeaway: In speech, je vais /vizite/ and j'ai /vizite/ differ only by vais vs. ai; in writing, vais takes -er and ai takes -é.
summary.curiosity_teaser: Up next on Le Pont ([18] Motion Takes être): see how Hier j'ai… Story Drills leads directly into Motion Takes être.

twist.prompt: Think it through again without looking back — express "Yesterday, I spoke with my friend and we ate at the restaurant" in French:
twist.target_answer: Hier, j'ai parlé avec mon ami et nous avons mangé au restaurant
twist.explanation: Re-constructing "Hier, j'ai parlé avec mon ami et nous avons mangé au restaurant" from the underlying rule cements the pattern of Hier j'ai… Story Drills.

mangé.etymology_derivation: manger ← Latin manducāre 'to chew'. English 'mange' is the eating disease — the verb came with the Normans' dogs.

parlé.etymology_derivation: parler ← Late Latin parabolāre 'to tell stories' — parable, parley, parliament (the talking-place).

visiter.etymology_derivation: visitation → visiter. The rare English noun unlocks the everyday verb: don't decide too quickly that you can't say it.

trouvé.etymology_derivation: trover 'to find' — what you found is a trove.

aimé.etymology_derivation: aimer ← ad + estimare 'to estimate'. English 'aim' drifted from the same estimate — aiming is assessing.

pris.etymology_derivation: French uses prendre ('to take') for ordering food and drink, just like English 'I'll take a coffee'.

vu.context_translation: I have already seen this film.
vu.etymology_derivation: English already owns this participle inside 'déjà vu'!

avec.etymology_derivation: ab hoc 'by this' wore into avec. No English twin — but 'with' itself once meant 'against', so prepositions travel too.
